title: Elastic microbatch ceiling and tenant-aware backpressure plan
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Problem: During sustained high QPS spikes we observe either elevated latency p95/p99 or sudden tail drops when the KV cache pressure drives aggressive eviction and the microbatch admission controller begins shedding. Current thresholds are static and tuned conservatively, leading to poor utilization or cascading latency when many low-priority tenants surge.

Goal: Implement an elastic microbatch ceiling with tenant-aware probabilistic shedding and a light-weight KV shadow-prioritization layer to (1) reduce p99 latency regressions under bursts, (2) improve GPU utilization for steady high QPS workloads, and (3) provide predictable graceful degradation per-tenant.

Scope: This ticket covers design, prototype implementation, instrumentation, canary rollout, and runbook updates for the admission controller, KV cache prioritization, and a conservative rollout plan. It does NOT include full multi-region routing changes or policy UI updates (those will be separate PM tickets).

Key ideas and decisions under consideration:
- Elastic ceiling: maintain a moving microbatch ceiling per-worker that adapts based on recent queue growth, GPU slot occupancy, and token emission rate. Ceiling updates use a bounded additive increase / multiplicative decrease (AIMD) policy to avoid oscillation.
- Tenant-weighted probabilistic shedding: when the worker is over headroom, requests are accepted with a probability that depends on tenant priority, recent success rate, and request estimated token length. This is cheaper than hard preemption and smooths acceptance rates across tenants.
- KV shadow prioritization: keep a small soft-mapped 'shadow' residency score for keys touched by high-priority tenants and short-lived sessions; the eviction policy uses a two-tier score combining frequency and tenant priority instead of pure LRU.
- Lightweight estimator for token-memory: augment admission decisions with a running estimator of KV memory per stream (approximate per-connection footprint) to avoid surprising spikes in GPU memory due to large contexts.

Acceptance criteria:
- New elastic ceiling controller reduces p99 generation latency by >= 20% during synthetic mixed-tenancy spike tests compared to baseline, without increasing overall token cost by >5%.
- No increase in observed OOM incidents in staging; GPU memory headroom metric must remain >= 8% during sustained load tests.
- Tenant SLOs: high-priority tenants experience <5% increase in tail latency and <1% request rejection in the worst-case synthetic scenarios; low-priority tenants can be probabilistically shed.
- Observability: dashboards added for per-worker ceiling, per-tenant acceptance probability, KV shadow residency heatmap, and headroom forecast.
- Runbook updated with clear mitigation steps and rollback toggles (per-worker debug flags and global feature flag).

Design notes and trade-offs:
- Why probabilistic shedding? Hard preemption requires moving work across workers and can cause costly cache misses. Probabilistic acceptance reduces worst-case amplification and is cheap to implement in the admission path.
- Cache prioritization vs strict reserved bytes: reserving bytes per-tenant would be more deterministic but increases fragmentation and reduces utilization. A shadow scoring approach aims for a middle-ground, improving hit-rate for high-priority flows without hard reservations.
- AIMD tuning is sensitive to workload patterns; we will pick conservative alpha/beta values and expose them as runtime knobs.

Implementation plan (week-by-week):
- Week 1 (this ticket): prototype elastic ceiling controller and per-worker metrics emission; add unit tests for AIMD logic.
- Week 2: implement tenant-weighted acceptance probability in admission hotpath; add micro-bench for CPU overhead (goal <1% extra p99 accept latency).
- Week 3: KV shadow scoring prototype and eviction policy hook, plus integration tests exercising eviction under synthetic hot keys.
- Week 4: integration load tests (mixed-tenancy synthetic), dashboarding, and runbook. Canary rollout to <1% traffic, monitor 48h then ramp.

Rollout & monitoring plan:
- Feature gated by a runtime flag: "elastic_ceiling_v1". Start canary on a small fleet subset with internal-only traffic.
- Key metrics: per-worker ceiling size, acceptance_rate_by_tenant, batch_size_distribution, gpu_headroom_percent, kv_shadow_hit_rate, p50/p95/p99 latency by tenant.
- Alerting: fire when gpu_headroom_percent < 5% for >5min, or if p99 increases by >30% during rollout.

Testing plan:
- Unit tests for AIMD controller and probabilistic decision math (statistical properties).
- Perf microbench measuring accept path overhead with 100k synthetic requests.
- Staging end-to-end mixed-tenancy blast with a realistic blend of short and long contexts, with injected KV hot keys.

Documentation & links:
- Design doc (internal): https://drive.google.com/drive/fake-redwood-designs/elastic-ceiling-v1
- Related PR template: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pulls/elastic-ceiling-proto
- Related tickets: ENG-7421 (adaptive microbatching), ENG-902468 (burst-tolerant admission).

Rollback strategy:
- Toggle runtime flag off to revert to previous static thresholds.
- If OOMs occur, immediately set per-worker max_microbatch to a safe floor and divert traffic by routing policy.

Open questions (to be resolved in design review):
- Exact AIMD parameters (alpha, beta, probe interval) and warm-start heuristic when a worker restarts.
- Whether to incorporate model-specific token emission profiles into ceiling calculations (models with faster token emission may need tighter ceilings).
- UI controls for tenant priority: expose simple tiers (high/normal/low) or numeric weights?
